section_1.title: Hook & The Prerequisite: Light's Speed in Vacuum
section_1.content: Start with a 30-second visual hook showing a 'broken' straw in a glass of water. Briefly recap that light travels at a constant speed (c) in a vacuum, which serves as our baseline reference.
section_1.example: An archerfish hunting: It must account for the shift in perceived position to hit its prey through the water-air interface.

section_2.title: Defining Refractive Index (n)
section_2.content: Introduce the refractive index as a measure of 'optical density.' Use a graphical representation: A runner (light) moving on a track (vacuum) vs. moving through deep sand (a dense medium). The formula n = c / v is displayed as a simple ratio.
section_2.example: Comparing light passing through air (n≈1) vs. diamond (n≈2.42), showing the corresponding 'speed limit' reduction in the material.

section_3.title: Snell’s Law: The Geometric Rule
section_3.content: Visualize the bending process. Use a 2D animation of a wavefront (represented by parallel lines) hitting a boundary at an angle. As one side hits the medium first and slows down, the entire 'wavefront' pivots.
section_3.example: A marching band turning a corner: When the soldiers on the inside slow down, the whole line automatically pivots toward the slower medium.

section_4.title: Mathematical Visualization
section_4.content: Present Snell's Law (n1 * sin(θ1) = n2 * sin(θ2)). Instead of just text, use an interactive-style overlay showing the angles θ1 and θ2 changing in real-time as the light beam rotates toward or away from the 'normal' line.
section_4.example: A laser pointer shining from air into a glass prism, showing the relationship between the incident angle and the refracted angle on a coordinate grid.

section_5.title: Real-World Application & Summary
section_5.content: Conclude by connecting the theory to human vision and technology. Summarize that refraction is the basis for all lens-based devices.
section_5.example: The human eye: How the cornea and lens refract incoming light to focus a sharp image onto the retina, much like a camera lens focusing light onto a sensor.
